items.explanation: The passage says clocks measure duration while memory measures meaning, so a year of grief can feel longer than a decade of routine, and time is not a single river but a set of rhythms. It does not claim time is purely subjective, that clocks are useless, or that the past and future are identical.
options: Time is purely subjective and clocks measure nothing at all
Time is a single river that flows at the same speed for everyone
Clocks measure duration while memory measures meaning, so the same length of time can feel very different depending on what filled it
Time is identical in the past, the present and the future, so memory is irrelevant
Clocks are useless because no one ever experiences time as passing
items.passage: We say that time passes, as if it were a river carrying us along, but the metaphor hides how many different times we actually live in. There is clock time, measured in seconds and deadlines, and there is lived time, measured in waiting, in boredom, in sudden joy. A year of grief can feel longer than a decade of routine. An afternoon with a friend can pass in what seems like minutes, while an afternoon in a queue can stretch into hours. The difference is not in the clocks, which tick at the same rate, but in attention and memory. Time feels long when it is filled with new experiences that memory must record, and short when it is filled with repetition that memory discards. This is why childhood summers seem endless and adult years seem to accelerate: childhood is dense with firsts, adulthood with routine. Philosophers have argued for centuries about whether time is real or an invention of the mind, but the practical question is different. It is how we should spend the time we have, given that its felt length depends on how we live it. A life filled with novelty, attention and reflection will feel longer in retrospect, even if it lasts the same number of years. A life of unexamined routine will feel short, not because it was, but because so little of it was noticed. The implication is unsettling. We cannot add years to a life, but we can add life to years, by breaking routine, by paying attention, and by remembering deliberately. Time, in this account, is not only something that happens to us. It is something we make, in the small choices of what to notice, what to repeat, and what to allow ourselves to forget. Calendars and deadlines impose clock time on lived time, and much of modern anxiety comes from the collision between the two. A project that takes a week on paper may take a month in lived experience, because it involves waiting, uncertainty and the slow work of thinking, none of which appears on a schedule. Managers who treat the schedule as reality may conclude that workers are lazy, when in fact they are living in a different kind of time. A more humane approach would allow for both kinds of time, setting deadlines that respect the rhythm of the work, and recognising that some tasks, like writing or designing, cannot be hurried without being damaged. That recognition does not make deadlines disappear, but it makes them honest, and honesty about time is the beginning of honesty about work.
items.question: According to the passage, why does the same length of clock time feel different in different lives?
items.set_title: RC1: Philosophy of Time and Memory

items.explanation: The passage says childhood is dense with firsts while adulthood is routine, so childhood summers seem endless and adult years accelerate in memory. It does not claim children have more clock time, that adults remember more, or that routine lengthens felt time.
options: Childhood is dense with first experiences that memory records, while adulthood is filled with routine that memory discards, so childhood feels longer in retrospect
Children have more hours in a day than adults do
Adults remember far more of each year than children do
Routine makes time feel longer, while novelty makes it feel shorter
Childhood summers were actually longer in the past than they are today
items.question: Why, according to the passage, do childhood summers seem endless while adult years seem to accelerate?
items.set_title: RC1: Philosophy of Time and Memory

items.explanation: The author says we cannot add years but can add life to years by breaking routine, paying attention and remembering deliberately. Seeking only novelty at any cost, repeating routine, and forgetting deliberately all misstate the advice, and the passage does not promise literal extra years.
options: By seeking only extreme novelty and avoiding all routine at any cost
By repeating the same routine every day so that memory has less to record
By forgetting deliberately everything that has happened
By living longer in clock time, which is the only way to add life to years
By breaking routine, paying attention, and remembering deliberately, so that more of life is noticed and retained
items.question: What does the author mean by adding life to years?
items.set_title: RC1: Philosophy of Time and Memory

items.explanation: The passage says trust is a bet on future behaviour made without full information, built slowly through repeated reliability and destroyed quickly by one betrayal, and that it allows cooperation without constant monitoring. It is not blind faith, a contract, or a guarantee.
options: Trust is blind faith that requires no evidence at all
Trust is a bet on future behaviour made without full information, built slowly through repeated reliability and destroyed quickly by betrayal
Trust is identical to a written contract and has the same legal force
Trust is a guarantee that the other person will never act against your interests
Trust is unnecessary in any society that has enough laws and police
items.passage: Trust is the most economical institution a society possesses, and also the most fragile. When trust is present, people can cooperate without constant monitoring, contracts can be short, and promises can be taken at face value. When it is absent, every transaction needs a lawyer, every promise needs a guarantee, and the cost of doing anything rises sharply. Trust is not the same as faith. It is a bet on future behaviour, made without full information, based on past reliability. It is built slowly, through repeated small acts of keeping one's word, and it is destroyed quickly, often by a single betrayal that rewrites the whole history in retrospect. Institutions face the same logic. A bank, a court or a newspaper does not earn trust by declaring itself trustworthy, but by behaving predictably over time, by admitting mistakes promptly, and by accepting scrutiny when it would rather not. The paradox is that trust, once lost, cannot be bought back by the same behaviour that built it. A bank that has failed its customers must do more than resume normal service; it must accept constraints it would not have accepted before, because the bet has changed. The depositor is no longer betting that the bank will behave well; she is betting that it cannot behave badly. Understanding this matters because trust is often treated as a mood, something that rises and falls with sentiment. In fact it is a structure, built of repeated actions and the expectations they create, and like any structure it can be maintained, neglected or deliberately demolished, but it cannot be wished back into existence. Banks after a crisis illustrate the point sharply, because they must persuade depositors to return, and depositors remember the failure longer than the recovery. A bank that resumes lending, publishes reassuring statements and sponsors community events may still find that trust returns slowly, because trust is not restored by the absence of failure but by the presence of constraint. Depositors want to see independent audits, limits on risk taking, and managers who accept lower pay when the bank performs poorly. Those constraints are costly and unwelcome, yet they are the price of rebuilding a structure that was demolished, and a bank that refuses to pay it may find that its customers have moved on, not in anger but in quiet, permanent caution.
items.question: How does the passage define trust?

items.explanation: The passage says a failed bank must accept constraints it would not have accepted before, because the depositor is now betting it cannot behave badly rather than that it will behave well. Resuming normal service, declaring trustworthiness and hiding mistakes are all presented as insufficient.
options: By resuming normal service exactly as before, as if nothing had happened
By declaring itself trustworthy in a public advertisement
By hiding its mistakes so that customers do not learn of them
By accepting constraints it would not have accepted before, so that customers bet it cannot behave badly rather than that it will behave well
By raising its prices so that only trusting customers remain
items.question: According to the passage, how can an institution that has lost trust begin to rebuild it?

items.explanation: The passage says trust is a structure built of repeated actions and expectations, which can be maintained, neglected or demolished but not wished back. It is not a mood, a feeling that returns on its own, or a purely legal matter.
options: Trust is a mood that rises and falls with public sentiment and returns on its own
Trust is a feeling that can be restored by a single apology, however insincere
Trust is a structure built of repeated actions and the expectations they create, which can be maintained, neglected or demolished but cannot be wished back
Trust is a purely legal concept with no connection to behaviour
Trust, once lost, can always be bought back by spending enough on advertising
items.question: Why does the author say trust is a structure rather than a mood?

items.explanation: The passage says debt transfers resources from the future to the present and lets a generation enjoy now what a later generation must repay, so the question is whether the borrowing creates assets the future can use. Debt is not free money, not always bad, and not only a government matter.
options: Debt is free money, because it never has to be repaid by anyone
Debt is always bad, regardless of what it is used to pay for
Debt affects only governments and never affects ordinary households
Debt is a way of borrowing from the past, since past generations pay for present spending
Debt transfers resources from the future to the present, so the key question is whether it creates assets the future can use to repay it
items.passage: Debt is often discussed as if it were a technical matter, a question of interest rates and repayment schedules. In fact it is a moral question disguised as a technical one. To borrow is to transfer resources from the future to the present, to enjoy now what a later generation must pay for. That transfer can be justified, when the borrowing creates something the future can use: a railway, a school, a hospital, a skill. It is harder to justify when the borrowing pays for consumption that leaves nothing behind, a feast today and a bill tomorrow. The difficulty is that the future cannot negotiate. It has no vote, no voice and no representative at the table where the borrowing is decided. The present generation therefore acts as both borrower and judge, and it is unsurprising that it often judges in its own favour. This is why rules about debt matter. A household that borrows to educate a child is making a different choice from a household that borrows to fund a holiday, even if the interest rate is the same. A government that borrows to build infrastructure is making a different choice from one that borrows to pay today's salaries. The numbers look similar; the moral content does not. None of this means debt should be avoided. A society that never borrows may also be a society that never builds. It means debt should be judged not by its size alone but by what it leaves behind, and by whether the generation that must repay it would have agreed to the bargain if it had been asked. Student loans are a clear example, because a young person borrows against a future income that does not yet exist, to pay for an education whose value is uncertain. If the education leads to a good job, the debt may be justified, and the future self may thank the present self for the gamble. If it does not, the debt becomes a burden that shapes every later choice, delaying marriage, home ownership and further study. The borrower, at eighteen, cannot know which outcome will occur, and the lender, who profits either way, has little incentive to warn her. A fair system would share the risk, so that the institution that benefits from the borrowing also bears some of the cost when the gamble fails, rather than leaving the entire burden on the person least able to bear it.
items.question: What is the author's central claim about debt?
items.set_title: RC3: The Political Economy of Debt

items.explanation: The passage contrasts borrowing for a railway, school or hospital with borrowing for consumption that leaves nothing behind, and says the numbers may look similar while the moral content differs. Interest rate alone, size alone, and the identity of the lender are not the test proposed.
options: Whether the interest rate is low or high
Whether the borrowing creates something the future can use, rather than paying for consumption that leaves nothing behind
Whether the borrower is a government or a household
Whether the debt is large or small in absolute terms
Whether the lender is a bank or a private individual
items.question: According to the passage, how should debt be judged?
items.set_title: RC3: The Political Economy of Debt

items.explanation: The passage says the future has no vote, no voice and no representative, so the present acts as both borrower and judge and often judges in its own favour. The future is not said to be wealthy, indifferent, or represented by banks.
options: The future has no vote, no voice and no representative at the table, so the present generation acts as both borrower and judge
Future generations are wealthier than the present and can easily repay any debt
Future generations do not care what the present generation borrows
Banks always represent the interests of future generations fairly
Debt is never a moral question, only a technical one
items.question: Why does the author say borrowing from the future is morally difficult?
items.set_title: RC3: The Political Economy of Debt

items.explanation: The passage says science advances by stating uncertainty plainly, that uncertainty is a measure of knowledge, and that the public mistake is treating a range as ignorance rather than precision. It does not say scientists know nothing, that uncertainty means failure, or that experts should hide ranges.
options: Uncertainty means scientists know nothing at all about a subject
Uncertainty is a sign that a scientific field has failed and should be abandoned
Uncertainty is a measure of what is known, stated as a range, and treating a range as ignorance mistakes precision for weakness
Uncertainty should always be hidden from the public, because the public cannot understand it
Uncertainty disappears entirely once a study has been published in a journal
items.passage: Science is often presented as a body of certain facts, and scientists are often punished, in public debate, for admitting that they do not know. That punishment misunderstands how science works. A scientist who says a result is likely, within a range, is not being evasive; she is being precise. Uncertainty, stated honestly, is a measure of what is known, not a confession of ignorance. The public difficulty is that uncertainty feels like weakness. A politician who says we do not yet know is accused of dithering, while a politician who claims certainty is praised for leadership, even when the certainty is false. The result is a perverse incentive: those who know most about a subject are the most careful in their claims, while those who know least are the most confident. Expertise, in this account, is not the ability to give a single number without hesitation. It is the ability to say what is known, what is not known, and what would change the answer. A good expert is therefore recognisable not by confidence but by the quality of her doubts. She can name the evidence that would prove her wrong, and she updates her view when that evidence arrives. The test of expertise is not whether a person is ever wrong, since all experts are sometimes wrong, but whether they are wrong in a way that can be corrected, and whether they welcome the correction when it comes. Climate models illustrate the same point in a different register, because they produce ranges, not single numbers, and those ranges are often reported as if they were a failure of knowledge. A model that predicts warming of between one and a half and three degrees is not saying that scientists do not know what will happen; it is saying that the outcome depends on choices that have not yet been made, about emissions, about policy and about technology. That is a precise statement, and it is more honest than a single number that pretends the future is already decided. The public, however, often hears the range as uncertainty, and uncertainty as an excuse for inaction, when in fact the range is a call to action, because the lower end is available only if choices change, and the upper end is the price of doing nothing.
items.question: According to the passage, what is the proper role of uncertainty in science?

items.explanation: The passage says those who know most are most careful while those who know least are most confident, because uncertainty feels like weakness and certainty is praised even when false. It does not claim experts are always wrong, that confidence proves knowledge, or that politicians understand science better.
options: Experts are always wrong, while confident amateurs are always right
Confidence is the best test of whether a person is an expert
Politicians understand science better than scientists do
Those who know most about a subject are the most careful in their claims, while those who know least are the most confident, because certainty is rewarded even when false
Uncertainty should be punished in public debate because it shows weakness
items.question: What perverse incentive does the passage identify in public debate about science?

items.explanation: The author says a good expert can name the evidence that would prove her wrong and updates when it arrives, and the test is whether she is wrong in a correctable way and welcomes correction. Never being wrong, refusing to change, and hiding doubts all contradict that test.
options: By whether she is ever wrong, since a true expert is never wrong
By whether she refuses to change her view when new evidence arrives
By whether she hides her doubts from the public
By whether she speaks with complete confidence at all times
By whether she can name the evidence that would prove her wrong and welcomes correction when it arrives
items.question: How, according to the author, can a good expert be recognised?

items.explanation: The passage says some words carry a history, a joke or a grief that has no equivalent, so translation can convey meaning while losing the life around the word, and a good translator must choose what to preserve and what to let go. It does not say translation is impossible, that dictionaries are sufficient, or that languages are identical.
options: Translation is impossible, because no word can ever be carried from one language to another
Some words carry a history, a joke or a grief that has no equivalent, so a translation can convey the meaning while losing the life around the word
All languages have exactly the same words for the same things, so translation is mechanical
A dictionary is sufficient for translation, and no judgement is ever required
Translation never loses anything, because meaning is independent of language
items.passage: Every language has words that refuse to travel. They carry a history, a joke, a grief or a season that has no equivalent in another tongue, and when they are translated, something is lost that no footnote can fully restore. A word for the smell of rain on dry earth, for the light of a particular afternoon, for a form of respect owed to an elder, may be rendered accurately and still feel empty, because the life around the word has not travelled with it. This does not mean translation is impossible. It means translation is a choice, not a mechanical transfer. The translator must decide what to preserve and what to let go: the literal meaning, the rhythm, the association, the joke. Each choice saves one thing and sacrifices another, and a good translation is honest about the sacrifice it has made. Cultures, like languages, lose something in every act of translation, and gain something too. A story that travels acquires new readers, new meanings and new lives, even as it leaves behind the particular soil in which it grew. The loss is real, and it should be mourned, but the gain is real as well, and it should be celebrated. To refuse translation for fear of loss would be to keep every culture locked in its own room, and to translate carelessly, pretending nothing is lost, would be to lie about what has happened. The honest position is in between: to translate with care, to name what has been lost, and to allow the translated work to live a second life that is different from, but not lesser than, the first. Film subtitles show the same trade off in miniature, because a translator must decide whether to preserve the literal words, the joke, the rhythm or the cultural reference, and cannot preserve them all. A joke that depends on a pun may be replaced by a different joke, a reference to a local celebrity may be replaced by a reference the audience will recognise, and a formal speech may be rendered in slang to preserve its tone. Viewers who compare the subtitle with the original may complain that something has been lost, and they are right, but they may miss what has been gained, which is a film that can be understood and enjoyed by people who do not speak the language. Translation, in this sense, is not a failure to be perfect, but a success in being useful, and usefulness requires choice.
items.question: What is the author's central claim about untranslatable words?

items.explanation: The passage says translation is a choice, not a mechanical transfer, and the translator must decide what to preserve and what to let go, each choice saving one thing and sacrificing another. A mechanical word swap, a footnote restoring everything, and preserving everything at once are all rejected.
options: Translation is a mechanical transfer in which every word has an exact equivalent
A footnote can fully restore everything that is lost in translation
Translation is a choice in which the translator decides what to preserve and what to let go, saving one thing and sacrificing another
A good translation preserves everything at once, with no sacrifice at all
Translation requires no judgement, because dictionaries decide every choice
items.question: According to the passage, what does a translator actually do?

items.explanation: The author says the honest position is to translate with care, name what has been lost, and allow the work a second life different from but not lesser than the first. Refusing translation and pretending nothing is lost are both rejected, and mourning alone is not the position proposed.
options: Translate with care, name what has been lost, and allow the translated work a second life different from but not lesser than the first
Refuse all translation for fear of loss, keeping every culture locked in its own room
Translate carelessly while pretending that nothing has been lost
Mourn the loss but never celebrate the gain that translation brings
Preserve only the literal meaning and ignore rhythm, association and joke
items.question: What honest position does the author propose toward translation?

items.explanation: The poem shows her father drawing maps of a river that moved, a border that shifted, and a house that was no longer there, teaching her that maps are promises, not facts, and that a place can be lost on paper before it is lost on the ground. The other readings ignore the shifting river and border or invent a literal complaint.
options: Her father was a poor mapmaker who could not draw accurate maps
Her father drew maps to impress his neighbours with his skill
Her father was trying to sell maps for money
Her father drew maps of a river that moved and a border that shifted, teaching her that maps are promises rather than facts
Her father believed that maps could prevent rivers from changing course
items.passage: My father drew maps of a river that moved, / of a border that shifted in the night, / of a house that stood where the road now bends, / and of a village that was no longer there. // He drew them in pencil, so they could be changed, / and taught me to read the dotted lines, / the places where the map admitted it did not know, / the small, honest gaps where the land had moved on. // But at home I learned that a map is a promise, / and broken by the land itself, in its own time. // Now I draw maps of my own, / and I leave the dotted lines in, on purpose, / because a place, like a person, is never finished, / and the honest map is the one that says, / here, I do not know, and here, I am still learning.
items.question: What does the father's mapmaking chiefly teach the speaker?

items.explanation: Leaving dotted lines in on purpose shows a deliberate honesty about incompleteness, matching the father's pencil maps and the admission of not knowing. It is not laziness, a lack of skill, or a belief that maps are useless.
options: She is too lazy to finish her maps properly
She deliberately leaves gaps to show honesty about what is unfinished and unknown, as her father did
She does not know how to draw a complete map
She believes maps are useless and should not be drawn at all
She is copying her father's maps exactly without understanding them
items.question: The speaker's decision to leave dotted lines in her own maps most nearly suggests that

items.explanation: The argument moves from a correlation between sleep and grades to a causal claim, so it must assume sleep itself causes the grades rather than a third factor like motivation or study habits explaining both. The other options are stronger claims the argument does not need.
options: All students who sleep eight hours get top grades
Sleep itself causes the higher grades, rather than other differences such as motivation or study habits that also explain both
Students who sleep less never study at all
Sleep is the only factor that affects academic performance
Eight hours is the exact amount of sleep every student needs
items.question: A study finds students who sleep eight hours a night get higher grades than students who sleep six hours. A headteacher concludes that requiring eight hours of sleep will raise grades. Which assumption is required?

items.explanation: If the price rise coincided with a fall in the price of a close substitute, customers may have switched for price reasons rather than because of the advertisement, offering an alternative cause. Customer liking, the ad being memorable, and sales rising in another city are weaker or irrelevant.
options: Some customers said they liked the new advertisement
The advertisement was shown on television every evening
Sales also rose in a city where the advertisement was not shown
The advertisement won an award for creativity
The price rise coincided with a fall in the price of a close substitute, so customers may have switched for price reasons
items.question: A shop raises its prices and launches a new advertisement, and sales rise by 20 percent. The owner argues the advertisement caused the rise. Which finding most weakens the argument?

items.explanation: Because the runners also eat differently and sleep more, those differences could explain the lower illness rate, so the study cannot establish that running alone caused it. It does not prove running has no effect, nor that non-runners will always fall ill.
options: The study cannot establish that running alone caused the difference, because the runners also differed in diet and sleep
Running alone causes lower illness rates, regardless of diet and sleep
Running has no effect on health at all
People who do not run will always fall ill more often
Diet and sleep are irrelevant to illness
items.question: A study finds people who run regularly fall ill less often than people who do not. However, the runners also eat more vegetables and sleep more. Which conclusion is best supported?

items.explanation: Pusillanimous means lacking courage, timid, so cowardly is closest. Brave and bold are opposites, generous concerns giving rather than courage, and resolute means determined, which is also the opposite of timid.
options: Brave
Bold
Cowardly
Generous
Resolute
items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to PUSILLANIMOUS.

items.explanation: Either or takes the nearer subject, the teacher, which is singular, so is is correct, while the other options mismatch singular and plural subjects. Each takes was, and neither the teacher nor the students takes were, not was, so those distractors fail on agreement.
options: Either the students or the teacher were responsible for the error.
Either the students or the teacher are responsible for the error.
Either the students or the teacher is responsible for the error.
Each of the students was responsible for the error.
Neither the teacher nor the students was responsible.
items.question: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

items.explanation: The order must open with the invention, then its promise, then the queue of waiting readers, then the machine breaking, then the lesson about the last copy, giving B, D, A, C, E. Starting with E states the lesson first, and C before A breaks the machine before readers queue.
options: B, A, D, C, E
A, B, D, C, E
E, B, D, A, C
B, D, A, C, E
D, B, A, E, C
items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) Within a week, a queue of readers stretched around the block. (B) The inventor built a machine that could print a book in a minute. (C) On the eighth day, the machine broke, and the queue dispersed in silence. (D) He promised that no one would ever have to wait for a book again. (E) The last copy, he learned, is the one that is never printed. Choose the correct order.

items.explanation: The sequence runs from the farmer planting, to the rain failing, to the well running dry, to the neighbours sharing water, to the lesson that a village is a well, giving A, B, C, D, E. Any opening other than A puts an effect before its cause, and E before D states the lesson before the sharing that proves it.
options: A, C, B, D, E
B, A, C, D, E
E, A, B, C, D
A, B, D, C, E
A, B, C, D, E
items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The farmer planted his field in March, as his father had done before him. (B) The rains failed in April, and the sky stayed empty for weeks. (C) By June, the well had run dry, and the field was dust. (D) The neighbours shared their water, a little each day, until the rains returned. (E) A village, the farmer learned, is not a place but a well that is shared. Choose the correct order.

items.explanation: The sentence needs a word for harsh criticism and a word for praise: vituperative for the attack and laudatory for the praise fits, while the other pairs mix praise with praise or criticism with criticism in the wrong places. Acrimonious is close but laudatory is the precise counterpart, and vituperative is stronger than acrimonious here.
options: vituperative and laudatory
laudatory and vituperative
acrimonious and laudatory
vituperative and acrimonious
laudatory and commendatory
items.question: Fill in the blanks with the most appropriate pair. The review was ______ in its attack on the novel, yet ______ in its praise of the author's earlier work, leaving readers unsure which book to trust. (1) vituperative (2) laudatory (3) acrimonious (4) commendatory

items.explanation: A man climbing a ladder labelled Success toward a cloud while the ladder stands on a pile of books labelled Failure shows that success is built on earlier failures, not on avoiding them. The literal readings miss the labels, and the cloud being dangerous or the books being heavy are not the point.
options: Success requires avoiding all failure at any cost
Books are too heavy to use as a foundation for a ladder
Clouds are dangerous and should not be climbed toward
Success is often built on earlier failures, which provide the foundation for later achievement
The man should climb down immediately because the ladder is unsafe
items.question: The cartoon shows a man climbing a tall ladder labelled Success toward a cloud, while the ladder stands on a large pile of books labelled Failure. The man is smiling and looking up, not down at the books. What message does the cartoon most likely convey?

items.explanation: If print readers are older and shrinking while digital readers are younger and growing, the future audience is digital, which supports investing in the digital edition despite the current print profit. Print advertising being stable would argue against change. A rival closing is a temporary gain. A new press would lock money into print. A government grant for print would support keeping print.
options: Print advertising revenue has been stable for the last three years
A rival newspaper closed last year, leaving its readers to choose a new paper
Print readers are mostly over 60 and shrinking by 8 percent a year, while digital readers are mostly under 40 and growing by 15 percent a year
The paper has just bought a new printing press with a ten-year life
The state government offers a grant for newspapers that keep a print edition
items.passage: A 90-year-old regional newspaper has seen its print circulation fall from 4 lakh copies a day to 2.4 lakh in five years, while its free website reaches 30 lakh readers a month but earns only a tenth of the revenue per reader that print earns. The print edition still makes a profit because of loyal older readers and local advertising, but the printing press is 30 years old and needs a 6 crore rupee replacement. The editor wants to close the print edition within two years and move fully digital, arguing that the future audience is online and that the press replacement money should fund digital journalism instead. The circulation head warns that closing print would lose the most loyal readers, who pay the highest price, and that digital advertising rates are falling as social media takes the market. The advertising head notes that local businesses still prefer print ads because they trust the paper, while national advertisers have already moved online. The owner must decide before the press replacement contract is signed, because the contract commits the firm for ten years. A survey shows that 70 percent of print readers are over 55, while 80 percent of website readers are under 40, and that website readers spend an average of four minutes a day on the site compared with 40 minutes for print readers. The website earns money from display advertising, but rates have fallen by a third in two years as advertisers move to social media. The paper's loyal print readers include many local businesses that have advertised for decades and who say they trust the paper more than any other local medium. The digital team has 25 journalists and wants funding for video reporting and data journalism that the print edition cannot support.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support moving fully digital within two years?
items.set_title: DM1: The Newspaper at a Crossroads

items.explanation: A hybrid model with a slimmed print edition for loyal readers and a paid digital product protects both revenue streams and buys time to learn what digital readers will pay for. Closing print at once loses the loyal base. Keeping print unchanged ignores the falling circulation. Making the website free removes the only digital revenue. Selling the press and renting it back is a financial trick that does not solve the audience problem.
options: Close the print edition immediately and make the website free for all readers
Keep the print edition unchanged and sign the ten-year press contract
Sell the printing press and rent it back from the buyer
Run a slimmed-down print edition for loyal readers alongside a paid digital edition with exclusive local reporting, and review the mix after one year
Stop all digital investment and focus only on print advertising
items.question: What should the owner do before signing the press contract?
items.set_title: DM1: The Newspaper at a Crossroads

items.explanation: If digital readers pay for other news sites, the claim that digital readers will never pay is false, which directly weakens the case against a paid digital edition. Print readers being loyal supports print but does not show digital readers will not pay. A rival closing print is a precedent, not a weakness. Falling ad rates support the editor. A new press being cheaper does not address reader willingness to pay.
options: Print readers are the most loyal readers the paper has
A rival newspaper closed its print edition last year
Digital advertising rates are falling across the industry
A new printing press would cost less than expected
Two in five digital readers of this paper already pay for at least one other news website
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the circulation head's argument that digital readers will never pay for news?
items.set_title: DM1: The Newspaper at a Crossroads

items.explanation: If the product was sold as low risk to people who needed safe savings, the mis-selling is clear and the case for full compensation and disclosure is strongest. The staff following a script shows a system failure, not an excuse. A rival selling the same product does not make this sale fair. Bonuses for selling explain the motive but do not justify the sale. The product being legal does not make the way it was sold honest.
options: The product was sold as low risk to retired customers who needed safe savings and could not afford to lose money
The staff who sold the product followed the script given by head office
A rival bank sells the same product to its customers
Staff received a bonus for selling this product
The product itself is legal and approved by the regulator
items.passage: A large private bank sold a complex investment product to 12,000 retail customers over two years, describing it in brochures as a safe alternative to fixed deposits. The product in fact carried a risk of losing up to 30 percent of the invested amount if a stock index fell, a risk buried in the fine print on page 14 of the agreement. Around 3,000 customers, many of them retired, have lost money and filed complaints, and the regulator has asked the bank for an explanation. The bank's retail head argues that the risk was disclosed in the agreement, that customers signed it, and that the bank should fight the complaints in court rather than pay compensation, because paying would invite claims from all 12,000 buyers. The compliance head warns that the marketing material was misleading, that the regulator can impose a large fine, and that fighting retired customers in court will damage the bank's reputation for years. The chief executive must decide this week, because the regulator has set a deadline for the bank's response and a consumer group is planning a public protest outside the bank's head office. The consumer group has collected 2,000 complaints and plans a protest outside the head office on Friday. The regulator has set a deadline of one week for the bank's response and has the power to fine the bank and to order compensation. The retail head has warned the board that paying all 12,000 buyers would cost far more than paying the 3,000 who complained, while the compliance head has warned that fighting in court could take five years and would keep the story in the news throughout.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support paying full compensation to the affected customers?

items.explanation: If the misleading description was used in training, the failure is systemic and the bank cannot blame individual staff or the fine print, which strengthens the case for a bank-wide remedy. Customers being wealthy would not make misleading sales acceptable. A court case being slow is a practical point, not a moral one. The regulator asking only for an explanation does not settle the duty. The product being popular elsewhere is irrelevant to how it was sold here.
options: Most of the affected customers are wealthy and can absorb the loss
The misleading description of the product as safe was used in the bank's own staff training material
A court case would take at least five years to conclude
The regulator has asked only for an explanation, not for compensation
The product is popular with customers in other countries
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support the compliance head's view that the bank's marketing was misleading?

items.explanation: The product being legal and the agreement being signed are arguments the retail head can use, but they do not show the marketing was honest, so they are not valid reasons to compensate. The fine print being buried, the retired customers' vulnerability, the regulator's power to fine, and the reputational damage from fighting in court are all genuine reasons to pay compensation.
options: The risk was buried in fine print on page 14 while the brochure called the product safe
Many affected customers are retired and cannot afford the loss
The product is legal and the customers signed the agreement
The regulator can impose a large fine for misleading marketing
Fighting retired customers in court will damage the bank's reputation for years
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to pay compensation to the affected customers EXCEPT

items.explanation: If the same material failed in two earlier buildings, the risk is known and proven, not theoretical, which makes using it again indefensible. The material being cheaper and the project being behind schedule are pressures, not justifications. The rival using it does not make it safe. A new test that has not been run cannot support the choice.
options: The cheaper material would save 2 crore rupees on the project
The project is already six months behind schedule
A rival builder uses the same material in its projects
The same material was linked to cracks in two earlier buildings built by this firm
A new test for the material has been announced but not yet run
items.passage: A construction firm is building a 20-storey residential tower with 400 flats, most of them already sold to families who have paid advances. The project manager has found that using a cheaper cement mix would save 2 crore rupees and help the firm meet its deadline, but the firm's own engineer has warned that the cheaper mix has not been tested for a building of this height and that the supplier cannot provide a full safety certificate. The firm's owner is under pressure from lenders to finish on time, and the sales team has promised buyers possession by December. The engineer wants to use the standard mix, which costs more and would delay the project by two months, and to inform buyers of the delay. The owner argues that the cheaper mix has been used in smaller buildings without problems, that the delay would cost the firm its reputation with buyers, and that the engineer is being overcautious. The structural consultant, who must sign the safety certificate, has said privately that the consultant will not sign if the cheaper mix is used. The buyers have paid advances of up to 40 lakh rupees each and many have taken home loans that they are already repaying. The lenders have said the loan will be reviewed if the project is delayed by more than two months. The structural consultant is an independent firm that has certified 30 towers in the city and has refused to sign certificates for two other builders who used cheaper materials. The firm's owner has built 12 residential projects in 20 years without a safety incident.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support using the standard mix despite the delay?

items.explanation: Informing buyers of a two-month delay, using the standard mix, and having the consultant certify safety protects buyers and the firm's long-term standing, while the delay is disclosed honestly. Using the cheaper mix without a certificate risks lives and liability. Hiding the mix, blaming the engineer, or offering a discount to buy silence all leave the safety risk in place.
options: Use the cheaper mix and do not tell the buyers
Use the cheaper mix and blame the engineer if problems appear later
Offer buyers a small discount in exchange for not asking about the materials
Delay the project by two months but use the cheaper mix anyway
Use the standard mix, inform buyers of the two-month delay with a clear reason, and obtain the structural consultant's safety certificate
items.question: What should the firm do?

items.explanation: If the cheaper mix is approved for buildings of this height in another country with the same standards, the engineer's caution about height may be misplaced, which weakens the case against the cheaper mix. The supplier being small and the mix being used in smaller buildings do not show it is safe at this height. A past fine and the consultant refusing to sign both strengthen the case for the standard mix.
options: The cheaper mix is approved for buildings of this height in another country with the same safety standards
The supplier is a small firm with no large clients
The cheaper mix has been used in smaller buildings without problems
The firm was fined five years ago for using substandard material
The structural consultant has said the consultant will not sign if the cheaper mix is used
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the engineer's argument against the cheaper mix?

items.explanation: If the donor's child scored far below the cut-off, admitting the child would be a clear breach of merit and would be indefensible if discovered. The donor offering to fund a library is a temptation, not a justification. A past donation and the admissions head being new do not change the merit facts. Other universities doing the same does not make it right.
options: The donor has offered to fund a new library for the university
The donor's child scored far below the published cut-off for admission
The donor gave a large gift to the university five years ago
The admissions head is new and wants to please the trustees
Other universities also admit a few donor children each year
items.passage: A well-known private university receives an application from the child of a major donor who has pledged 10 crore rupees for a new science block. The child scored well below the published cut-off for the university's flagship engineering programme, while 200 other applicants who scored above the cut-off were rejected for lack of seats. The vice-chancellor is under pressure from the trustees to admit the donor's child, arguing that the donation will fund laboratories that benefit thousands of students and that one seat will not be noticed. The admissions head argues that the university's prospectus promises admission on merit, that the rejected applicants include students from poor families who studied for years to clear the cut-off, and that the admission would leak and destroy the university's reputation. The donor has said privately that the donation depends on the admission, and the science block is already half built with money the university borrowed. The admissions committee must decide before the term starts in three weeks. The trustees include the donor, two alumni and three academics, and the vice-chancellor needs their support for the science block loan. The 200 rejected applicants include 40 students from poor families who scored above the cut-off after years of preparation, and their parents have written to the university asking how admissions are decided. The science block is half built and the university has borrowed 6 crore rupees to pay the builders, who have said they will stop work if the next payment is late. The admissions committee meets in two days and must publish its decision before the term starts.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support refusing the donor's child?

items.explanation: If the university has admitted donor children before and its ranking fell after the practice became known, the proposed admission is a proven reputational risk, not a safe secret. The science block being half built is a pressure, not a justification. The child being willing to work hard does not cure a merit breach. A single seat being small does not make the breach invisible. The donor's gift being the largest ever increases the temptation but does not change the merit issue.
options: The science block is already half built with borrowed money
The donor's child is willing to work hard and repeat the first year if needed
The university admitted donor children twice before, and its national ranking fell each time after the practice became public
One seat is a small share of the 500 seats in the programme
The donor's gift is the largest the university has ever received
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the vice-chancellor's argument that one seat will not be noticed?

items.explanation: Refusing the admission on merit, while offering the donor a transparent naming opportunity for the science block that is not linked to admission, protects the merit promise without losing the gift if the donor truly cares about the university. Admitting the child breaks the merit promise. Admitting secretly compounds the breach. Rejecting the donation outright loses a benefit that could be accepted on clean terms. Delaying leaves the seat and the funding unresolved.
options: Admit the donor's child immediately and keep it secret
Reject the donation outright and close the science block project
Admit the child but ask the donor to keep the admission confidential
Refuse the admission on merit, explain the policy publicly, and offer the donor a transparent naming opportunity for the science block that is not linked to any admission
Delay the decision until after the term starts
items.question: What should the admissions committee do?

items.explanation: If the scientist's absence would halt a project worth 30 crore rupees, the firm has a concrete commercial reason to act now rather than wait for the person to leave. The scientist being the only expert is the problem itself. A rival offering a higher salary explains the risk but does not show the cost. Junior staff being unhappy is a separate issue. The scientist having no written contract is a process gap, not evidence of the cost of losing the person.
options: The scientist is the only person in the firm who understands the core process
A rival firm has offered the scientist a higher salary
Junior staff are unhappy that the scientist gets special treatment
The scientist has no written employment contract
The scientist's absence for even a month would halt a project worth 30 crore rupees in orders
items.passage: A pharmaceutical research firm depends on one senior scientist who understands a complex drug synthesis process that no one else in the firm can reproduce. The scientist refuses to document the process, declines to train juniors, and has told the head of research that the knowledge is the scientist's own job security. The firm has offered the scientist a large pay rise, a promotion and a research budget, but the scientist has refused all of them and now wants a guarantee of lifetime employment in writing. The head of research warns that if the scientist falls ill or resigns, a project worth 30 crore rupees in orders will stop, and that the firm is effectively held hostage by one person. The human resources head argues that giving a lifetime guarantee would set a dangerous precedent and would be unfair to 200 other employees. The chief executive must decide before the scientist's current contract ends in two months, and the scientist has already been approached by two rival firms. The scientist joined the firm eight years ago and built the synthesis process from an idea in a research paper, working alone for three years before the first successful batch. The project is worth 30 crore rupees in orders from two large drug makers who have said they will move to a rival if deliveries stop. The scientist has been approached twice by rival firms and has told colleagues that the offers are attractive. The head of research has asked two junior scientists to try to reproduce the process, but both have said they need the senior scientist's notes, which do not exist.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support acting now to reduce the firm's dependence on the scientist?
items.set_title: DM5: The Scientist Who Will Not Share

items.explanation: If the scientist has already trained a junior in a pilot and the junior can now run part of the process, documentation and training are feasible, which weakens the idea that the knowledge cannot be shared. The scientist being near retirement increases urgency but does not show sharing is possible. A rival approach and a large pay rise do not address feasibility. The process being complex is the scientist's own argument for keeping it secret.
options: The scientist has already trained one junior in a pilot project, and that junior can now run part of the process alone
The scientist is close to retirement age
A rival firm has approached the scientist twice
The firm has offered the scientist a large pay rise
The process is highly complex and takes years to learn
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the scientist's claim that the process cannot be documented or taught?
items.set_title: DM5: The Scientist Who Will Not Share

items.explanation: The scientist refusing to train juniors is the core problem, not a reason to give in to the demand. The precedent risk, the unfairness to other employees, the risk of the project halting, and the rival approaches are all genuine reasons to refuse a lifetime guarantee and instead reduce dependence.
options: A lifetime guarantee would set a precedent that other employees would demand
The scientist refuses to train juniors or document the process
Giving the guarantee would be unfair to 200 other employees
The project would halt if the scientist leaves suddenly
Rival firms have already approached the scientist
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to refuse the scientist's demand for a lifetime employment guarantee EXCEPT
items.set_title: DM5: The Scientist Who Will Not Share

items.explanation: If the older staff hold the client relationships that generate most revenue, losing them would damage the business more than losing the younger staff, so the merger should protect them. The younger staff being cheaper to keep is a cost argument for the opposite choice. A new office and a past merger are not evidence about revenue. The union supporting the younger staff is a political fact, not a commercial one.
options: The younger staff are cheaper to employ than the older staff
The firm is opening a new office in another city next year
The older staff hold the client relationships that generate 70 percent of the merged firm's revenue
The last merger in this industry led to large layoffs
The union supports the younger staff in this dispute
items.passage: Two mid-sized accounting firms have merged, and the combined firm now has 40 partners and 300 staff doing the same work in two offices in the same city. The merger plan requires cutting 60 jobs to remove duplication, and the managing partners must choose who goes. One option is to retrench the 60 most recently hired staff, who are mostly under 30 and cheaper to employ, on a last-in-first-out basis. A second option is to retrench 60 older staff who are paid more and whose skills overlap most with the other firm's partners, which would save more money. A third option is to offer voluntary retirement to older staff with a generous package, and to retrain the rest. The younger staff argue that last-in-first-out punishes them for being new and for having no say in the merger. The older staff argue that they built the client base over decades and that losing them would lose clients. The union has warned that any forced retrenchment will lead to a legal challenge, and the merger agreement requires the combined firm to show a cost saving within one year. The merger agreement requires the combined firm to show a cost saving of 5 crore rupees within one year, and the managing partners have told the board the saving will come from removing duplication. The union has 200 members across the two firms and has warned that any forced retrenchment will be challenged in court, a process that could take two years. The older staff include 20 partners who have been with the firms for over 20 years, while the younger staff include 60 people hired in the last three years.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support choosing voluntary retirement for the older staff over forced retrenchment of the younger staff?

items.explanation: Voluntary retirement with a generous package, retraining for the rest, and a transparent selection process gives older staff a dignified exit, keeps the firm legally safe, and shows younger staff the process is fair. Forced retrenchment of the young punishes the newest staff. Forced retrenchment of the old loses client relationships. Deciding by office location is arbitrary. Doing nothing breaches the merger cost-saving requirement.
options: Retrench the 60 most recently hired staff immediately
Retrench 60 older staff by force and keep the younger staff
Decide who goes by which office building they sit in
Offer voluntary retirement to older staff with a generous package, retrain the remaining staff for the merged firm's needs, and publish the criteria used
Do nothing and hope the cost saving appears on its own
items.question: What is the best decision for the managing partners to take now?

items.explanation: If the older staff's clients follow the individuals rather than the firm, retrenching them loses the revenue the merger was meant to protect, which weakens the case for cutting older staff. The younger staff being cheaper and the older staff being paid more both support cutting older staff. A generous package makes voluntary exit affordable. The union warning applies to forced retrenchment generally, not specifically to older staff.
options: The younger staff are cheaper to employ than the older staff
The older staff are paid more than the younger staff
A generous voluntary package would cost less than a legal challenge
The union has warned of a legal challenge to any forced retrenchment
The older staff's clients say they would follow those individuals to another firm
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the case for retrenching the older staff?

items.explanation: If free users who try the premium features convert at a high rate, a free trial is a proven sales channel, which supports offering it rather than keeping features locked. A rival offering a free tier is competitive pressure but not proof. The support team being small is a cost to manage, not evidence of conversion. Investors wanting growth and users asking for a trial are wishes, not evidence that the trial works.
options: Free users who are given a 30-day trial of premium features convert to paying customers at a rate of 25 percent
A rival firm offers a free tier with most features included
The support team is small and already overloaded
Investors want the firm to grow faster this year
Free users have asked for a trial of the premium features
items.passage: A software firm sells a project management tool to small businesses. The tool has a free version with basic features and a premium version at 1,000 rupees a month with advanced reporting, integrations and priority support. Only 3 percent of free users upgrade to premium, and growth has stalled. The product head wants to make the premium features free for 30 days for all free users, arguing that users who try the features will see their value and pay. The finance head warns that giving premium features away will teach users to expect them for free, that support costs will rise, and that the 3 percent who currently pay may cancel and wait for the next free trial. The sales head suggests instead cutting the premium price by half, arguing that price is the barrier. The chief executive must decide before the next product release in six weeks, because the release locks the pricing page for the quarter and the firm has only enough cash for one major pricing change this year. The firm has 40,000 free users and 1,200 paying customers, and its cash will last for eight months at the current rate of spending. The support team has six people and already handles 200 tickets a day, mostly from free users asking for help with basic features. The sales head has argued that a price cut would bring in more paying customers quickly, while the finance head has warned that the firm cannot afford two pricing changes in one year. The product release in six weeks will lock the pricing page for the next quarter.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support offering the 30-day free trial of premium features?

items.explanation: A time-limited trial for new users only, with clear expiry and no extension, lets users experience the value without teaching existing payers to wait for a free period. A permanent free tier destroys the premium revenue. Cutting the price in half reduces revenue from existing payers. A trial for everyone including current payers invites cancellations. Doing nothing leaves the 3 percent conversion unchanged.
options: Make all premium features free permanently for every user
Offer a one-time 30-day trial of premium features to new free users only, with a clear expiry date and no extensions, while keeping the premium price unchanged for existing payers
Cut the premium price by half for all users
Offer the trial to existing paying customers as well so they can try new features
Make no change and keep the current pricing page
items.question: What should the chief executive do?

items.explanation: Rising support costs are a genuine cost of a trial, not a reason to reject it outright, and they can be managed, so this option is the exception among the criticisms. Teaching users to expect features for free, existing payers cancelling to wait, a trial that never converts, and locking the pricing page for a quarter are all valid criticisms of the trial proposal.
options: The trial may teach users to expect premium features for free
Existing paying customers may cancel and wait for the next free trial
The trial may attract users who never convert to paying customers
The pricing page is locked for a quarter after the release
Support costs will rise during the trial period
items.question: All of the following are valid criticisms of offering the free trial to all free users EXCEPT
A retailer buys a mixer for Rs 1500, marks it 80% above the cost price and sells it after a discount of 30% on the marked price. At what price does he sell the mixer?
items.explanation: The marked price is Rs 1500 x 1.80 = Rs 2700. A 30% discount leaves Rs 2700 x 0.70 = Rs 1889. The profit is Rs 389, but the question asks for the selling price, not the profit, so the profit figure and the marked price are both traps among the options.

items.question: A boat travels downstream at 24 km/h and upstream at 16 km/h in a river. What is the speed of the stream?
options: 8 km/h
2 km/h
6 km/h
20 km/h
4 km/h
items.explanation: Let the boat speed in still water be b and the stream speed be s. Then b + s = 24 and b - s = 16. Subtracting gives 2s = 8, so s = 4 km/h. The boat speed itself is 20.0 km/h, which is a tempting wrong option.

items.question: A vessel contains a mixture of milk and water in the ratio 7:3. If the total quantity of the mixture is 50 litres, how much milk does it contain?
options: 35 litres
20 litres
30 litres
40 litres
25 litres
items.explanation: The milk is 7/10 of the mixture, so it is 50 x 7/10 = 35 litres, and the water is 15 litres. The options that swap the two parts, or that take the ratio terms as litres, are wrong.

items.question: Six distinct positive integers have an average of 18. What is the maximum possible value of the largest integer?
items.explanation: The sum of all 6 values is 6 x 18 = 108. To make the largest value as big as possible, the other 5 values must be as small as possible while staying distinct and positive, so they are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, summing to 15. The largest value is therefore 108 - 15 = 93. Forgetting that the values must be distinct, or using the average itself as the maximum, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A is twice as efficient as B. B alone can finish a task in 18 days. In how many days will A and B together finish the task?
options: 9 days
12 days
4 days
7 days
6 days
items.explanation: Since A is twice as efficient, A alone takes 18/2 = 9 days. Together they do 1/9 + 1/18 = 1/6 of the task per day, so the time is 6 days. Taking A's time as 36 days, or adding the times, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A chord of length 12 cm is drawn in a circle of radius 10 cm. How far is the chord from the centre of the circle?
options: 6 cm
10 cm
4 cm
8 cm
12 cm
items.explanation: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 cm and one side 6 cm. The distance is sqrt(10 squared - 6 squared) = sqrt(64) = 8 cm. Using the full chord length as a side gives the wrong options.

items.question: A point inside a circle of radius 15 cm lies 9 cm from the centre. What is the length of the shortest chord of the circle passing through that point?
options: 30 cm
24 cm
18 cm
20 cm
15 cm
items.explanation: The shortest chord through the point is the one perpendicular to the line joining the point to the centre. Its half-length is sqrt(15 squared - 9 squared) = sqrt(144) = 12 cm, so the full chord is 24 cm. The longest chord is the diameter, 30 cm, which is a distractor.

items.question: What is the area of an equilateral triangle of side 12 cm?
options: 48√3 sq cm
24√3 sq cm
72√3 sq cm
36√3 sq cm
36 sq cm
items.explanation: The area of an equilateral triangle of side a is (sqrt(3)/4) x a squared. With a = 12, that is (sqrt(3)/4) x 144 = 36sqrt(3) sq cm. The options with the wrong coefficient, or with a plain number instead of a multiple of sqrt(3), are wrong.

items.question: A triangle has sides 7 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm. What is the length of the median drawn to the side of length 8 cm?
options: 6 cm
8 cm
9 cm
7 cm
5 cm
items.explanation: By Apollonius theorem, the median m to side 8 satisfies m squared = (2 x 7 squared + 2 x 9 squared - 8 squared)/4 = (98 + 162 - 64)/4 = 49. So m = 7 cm. The altitude and the semi-perimeter are different quantities and give the wrong options.

items.question: What is the total surface area of a cube of side 9 cm?
options: 324 sq cm
729 sq cm
486 sq cm
540 sq cm
432 sq cm
items.explanation: A cube has 6 faces, each of area 9 squared = 81 sq cm, so the total surface area is 6 x 81 = 486 sq cm. The volume is 729 cubic cm, which is a different quantity, and the area of one face alone is a distractor.

items.question: What is the highest common factor of 48 and 180?
items.explanation: 48 = 2 to the power 4 x 3 and 180 = 2 squared x 3 squared x 5, so the common factors are 2 squared x 3 = 12. The LCM is 720, which is a different quantity, and the other options are divisors that are not the highest.

items.question: What is the sum of all the positive divisors of 72?
items.explanation: The divisors of 72 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 72, and their sum is 195. Equivalently, from 72 = 2 cubed x 3 squared, the sum is (1+2+4+8) x (1+3+9) = 15 x 13 = 195. The number of divisors, or the sum of only the prime divisors, gives the wrong options.

items.question: How many three-digit numbers have digits that add up to 10?
items.explanation: Count triples (a, b, c) with a from 1 to 9, b and c from 0 to 9 and a + b + c = 10. Summing over the possible first digits gives 54 such numbers. Forgetting that the first digit cannot be zero, or counting all triples of digits summing to 10 without that restriction, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the smallest positive integer that has exactly 12 positive divisors?
items.explanation: A number with 12 divisors needs exponent patterns giving 12, such as 11, or 5 x 1, or 3 x 2, or 2 x 1 x 1. The smallest candidates are 2 to the power 11 = 2048, 2 to the power 5 x 3 = 96, 2 cubed x 3 squared = 72, and 2 squared x 3 x 5 = 60. The last is the smallest, so the answer is 60. The numbers 48 and 72 have 10 and 12 divisors respectively, but 48 has only 10 divisors.

items.question: If 2x + 3y = 12 and x - y = 1, what is the value of x + y?
items.explanation: From the second equation x = y + 1. Substituting gives 2(y + 1) + 3y = 12, so 5y = 10 and y = 2, hence x = 3. Then x + y = 3 + 2 = 5. Solving only one equation, or swapping x and y, gives the wrong options.

items.question: For x > 0, what is the minimum value of x + 9/x?
items.explanation: By AM-GM, x + 9/x is at least 2 sqrt(x x 9/x) = 2 x 3 = 6, with equality when x = 9/x, that is x = 3. The value at x = 1 or x = 9 is 10, which is larger, and the minimum is not attained at the endpoints.

items.question: One card is drawn at random from a standard pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that it is a king or a queen?
items.explanation: There are 4 kings and 4 queens, so 8 favourable cards out of 52, giving a probability of 8/52 = 2/13. Counting only the kings, or only one suit, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Let f(x) = x + 3 and g(x) = x squared. What is the value of g(f(4))?
items.explanation: First f(4) = 4 + 3 = 7, then g(7) = 7 squared = 49. Reversing the order of composition gives f(g(4)) = 16 + 3 = 19, which is a distractor, and applying only one function gives the other wrong options.

items.question: Is the integer y positive? Statement I: y squared = 25. Statement II: y is a prime number.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Either statement alone is sufficient.
Neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient.
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives y = 5 or y = -5, so it does not settle whether y is positive. Statement II alone means y is a prime, and every prime except none is positive, so y must be positive; in fact y = 5 is forced only with statement I, but positivity follows from statement II alone. Hence statement II alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is the total wheat production across the four states?

diagram.caption: Crop production (lakh tonnes) in four states, 2025

options: 370 lakh tonnes
440 lakh tonnes
390 lakh tonnes
410 lakh tonnes
460 lakh tonnes
items.explanation: Adding the wheat column gives 120 + 80 + 150 + 60 = 410 lakh tonnes. The total of another crop, or of a single state, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Which state has the highest total production of all three crops combined?
options: Punjab
Haryana
Uttar Pradesh
Madhya Pradesh
Two states tie for first
items.explanation: The combined totals are Punjab 250, Haryana 180, Uttar Pradesh 330 and Madhya Pradesh 135 lakh tonnes, so Uttar Pradesh is the highest. Punjab leads in no single crop, but the question asks for the combined total.

items.question: What is the average maize production per state?
options: 31 lakh tonnes
38.75 lakh tonnes
45 lakh tonnes
35 lakh tonnes
42 lakh tonnes
items.explanation: Total maize production is 155 lakh tonnes across 4 states, so the average is 155/4 = 38.75 lakh tonnes. The total itself, or the average of another crop, gives the wrong options.

items.set_title: DI2: Revenue of Two Product Lines
items.question: What is the total revenue of the company in 2024?

diagram.caption: Annual revenue (Rs crore) of two product lines, 2019-2024

options: Rs 300 crore
Rs 400 crore
Rs 330 crore
Rs 380 crore
Rs 350 crore
items.explanation: In 2024 Product A earned Rs 200 crore and Product B earned Rs 150 crore, so the total is Rs 350 crore. Either product alone, or the total of another year, gives the wrong options.

items.set_title: DI2: Revenue of Two Product Lines
items.question: In which year did Product A record its highest percentage growth over the previous year?
items.explanation: Product A's growth rates are 2020: 16.67%, 2021: -7.14%, 2022: 23.08%, 2023: 12.5% and 2024: 11.11%, so the highest is in 2022. The largest absolute increase is in a different year, but the question asks for percentage growth.

items.set_title: DI2: Revenue of Two Product Lines
items.question: What is the total revenue of Product B over the six years from 2019 to 2024?
options: Rs 600 crore
Rs 660 crore
Rs 720 crore
Rs 630 crore
Rs 750 crore
items.explanation: Adding Product B's yearly revenues gives 80 + 90 + 110 + 100 + 130 + 150 = Rs 660 crore. Product A's total is 930 crore, which is a distractor.

items.set_title: DI3: School Sections and Pass Rates
items.question: How many students passed in total across the three sections?

diagram.caption: Students and pass rates in three sections of a school
diagram.content: A school has three sections. Section A has 120 students with a pass rate of 90%. Section B has 100 students with a pass rate of 80%. Section C has 80 students with a pass rate of 70%.

options: 224 students
264 students
244 students
234 students
254 students
items.explanation: Students who passed are A: 108, B: 80 and C: 56, totalling 244. The total number of students is 300, which is a distractor.

items.set_title: DI3: School Sections and Pass Rates
items.question: What is the overall pass percentage of the school?
items.explanation: 244 of the 300 students passed, so the overall pass rate is 244/300 x 100 = 81.33%. Averaging the three section rates gives 80%, which is wrong because the sections have different sizes.

items.set_title: DI3: School Sections and Pass Rates
items.question: Which section has the largest number of students who failed?
options: Section A
Section B
Section C
Sections A and B
All three are equal
items.explanation: Failures are A: 12, B: 20 and C: 24, so Section C has the most failures. Section C has the lowest pass rate, which is why its failure count is highest despite being the smallest section.

items.question: The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for work on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits. Which trio shared the prize?
options: John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis
Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger
Pierre Agostini, Ferenc Krausz and Anne L'Huillier
Syukuro Manabe, Klaus Hasselmann and Giorgio Parisi
Roger Penrose, Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez
items.explanation: John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics for demonstrating macroscopic quantum tunnelling in electrical circuits. The Aspect trio won in 2022 for quantum entanglement, the Agostini trio in 2023 for attosecond pulses, the Manabe trio in 2021 for climate modelling, and the Penrose trio in 2020 for black holes.

items.question: Who won the men's singles title at Wimbledon in 2025?
options: Carlos Alcaraz
Jannik Sinner
Novak Djokovic
Daniil Medvedev
Alexander Zverev
items.explanation: Jannik Sinner won the 2025 Wimbledon men's singles title, beating defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in the final. Alcaraz finished runner-up, Djokovic lost in the semi-final, and Medvedev and Zverev were eliminated earlier in the tournament.

items.question: In December 2025, ISRO's LVM3 rocket carried its heaviest payload to date. Which satellite was it?
options: GSAT-20
NISAR
BlueBird Block-2
Chandrayaan-4
Aditya-L1
items.explanation: The BlueBird Block-2 communications satellite was launched on LVM3-M6 in December 2025 as the heaviest payload ever carried by the LVM3. NISAR was launched on a GSLV in July 2025, GSAT-20 flew on a Falcon 9 in 2024, Aditya-L1 flew on a PSLV in 2023, and Chandrayaan-4 has not yet been launched.

items.question: In the Bihar Assembly election held in November 2025, which alliance won a decisive majority?
options: Mahagathbandhan
Bahujan Samaj Party
All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen
National Democratic Alliance
Jan Suraaj Party
items.explanation: The National Democratic Alliance won a decisive majority in the Bihar Assembly election of November 2025, and Nitish Kumar continued as Chief Minister. The Mahagathbandhan was the main opposition, while Jan Suraaj won no seats and the Bahujan Samaj Party and AIMIM won only a handful between them.

items.question: Which novel won the Booker Prize in 2025?
options: Orbital by Samantha Harvey
James by Percival Everett
The Bee Sting by Paul Murray
Prophet Song by Paul Lynch
Flesh by David Szalay
items.explanation: Flesh by David Szalay won the Booker Prize in 2025. Orbital won in 2024, Prophet Song won in 2023, and James and The Bee Sting were shortlisted in earlier years but did not win the prize.

items.question: The Miss World 2025 pageant was held in which Indian city?
options: Hyderabad
Mumbai
New Delhi
Bengaluru
Jaipur
items.explanation: The Miss World 2025 pageant was held in Hyderabad, where Opal Suchata Chuangsri of Thailand was crowned the winner. Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru and Jaipur did not host the 2025 pageant.

items.question: Which country joined BRICS as a full member in January 2025?
options: Argentina
Indonesia
Egypt
Ethiopia
Nigeria
items.explanation: Indonesia joined BRICS as a full member in January 2025. Egypt and Ethiopia had joined in January 2024, Argentina declined its invitation to join, and Nigeria became a BRICS partner country in January 2025 rather than a full member.

items.question: Who was named Player of the Tournament at the ICC Champions Trophy 2025?
options: Rohit Sharma
Virat Kohli
Rachin Ravindra
Shreyas Iyer
Matt Henry
items.explanation: Rachin Ravindra of New Zealand was named Player of the Tournament at the 2025 Champions Trophy after scoring 263 runs, including two centuries. Rohit Sharma was Player of the Match in the final, Virat Kohli scored a century against Pakistan, Shreyas Iyer was India's leading run-scorer, and Matt Henry took 10 wickets.

items.question: Who or what was named Time magazine's Person of the Year for 2025?
options: Donald Trump
Taylor Swift
Elon Musk
The Architects of AI
Narendra Modi
items.explanation: The Architects of AI, the leaders building artificial intelligence, were named Time magazine's Person of the Year for 2025. Donald Trump was the 2024 choice, Taylor Swift the 2023 choice, Elon Musk the 2021 choice, and Narendra Modi has never been named Person of the Year.
